summary: For 9–10 year olds learning that dissolving, mixing, and changes of state are reversible (no new substance is made and the original material can be recovered). The core method is do-and-undo: perform a change, perform the action that reverses it, and confirm the SAME material has returned. Contrast this with an irreversible change (e.g. toasting bread) where a new substance forms. Emphasise conservation — the material persists even when it looks gone — and have learners judge by 'was a new substance made?' rather than by appearance or by whether heat was involved.
misconceptions: Melting or dissolving destroys or uses up the material.
All changes can be undone (over-generalising reversibility to burning/cooking).
A change of state makes a new substance rather than the same substance in a new state.
Mixing is irreversible because the materials 'became one thing'.
If a material looks different after a change, it must be a different material.

activities.title: The do-it, undo-it bench
steps: At station 1, gently warm a chunk of chocolate (e.g. in a bowl over warm water) only until it flows, then chill it and confirm it sets back into solid chocolate. Overheated chocolate can scorch or burn, which makes new substances and cannot be undone.
At station 2, stir salt into water until it seems to disappear (it is still there, dissolved), then gently heat the dish and confirm salt crystals reappear.

At station 3, tip sand into water, pour the mixture through a filter, and confirm the sand is separated out on the filter (damp, but the same sand) while the water passes through (it may be slightly cloudy if the sand has very fine particles).

For each station, do the change and then the reversing action, and check whether the same material has been recovered before moving on (if using a screen or bench simulation, this may be a forward/reverse control and a 'same material recovered?' indicator).

At a fourth station, an adult toasts a slice of bread; try to think of any action that would turn it back into bread and notice there is none ('you can't un-toast it — a new substance was made'). In a simulation, this may appear as a greyed-out reverse control.
Before testing each station, predict whether the change is reversible and say out loud the action that would reverse it.
activities.insight: A reversible change alters how a material looks or its state but makes NO new substance, so you can get the original material back by undoing it; some changes (toasting) make a new substance and cannot be undone.

activities.title: Reverse-arrow summary chart
steps: Match each change to its reversing action: melt⇄freeze, dissolve⇄evaporate, mix⇄filter.
Reveal or state what gets you back to the original material for each pair.
Add the single test that unites all three pairs: 'no new substance made'.
activities.insight: The canonical reversible changes — changes of state, dissolving, and mixing separable materials — all share one test: no new substance is formed, so the original can be recovered.

activities.title: Sort and justify: reversible or not?
steps: Categorise a set of changes as reversible or irreversible.
Match each reversible change to the specific action that would reverse it.
For each judgement, state the reason: can the original material be recovered, with no new substance made?
Tackle tricky cases: is dissolving salt reversible even though the water looks completely different? Is re-set chocolate the same substance?
activities.insight: Reversibility is judged by whether a new substance was made and the original can be recovered — not by whether heat was added or whether the material looks different.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain with chocolate
steps: Before any melting, predict: if we melt this chocolate in a bowl and then put it in the fridge, will we get chocolate back — and WHY?
State your reason out loud before observing (this reasoning is the important part).
Melt the chocolate, then let it set, and compare your prediction with what happened.

Answer probe questions: Is dissolving salt reversible even though it looks nothing like before? Would un-heating toast make it bread again, and why not? Then give your own test for 'reversible' that works no matter what the change looks like.
activities.insight: Stating the reason before observing surfaces whether a learner is reasoning from 'heating spoils it' or appearance versus the correct test of whether a new substance was made.

checkQuestion: Think of ice melting into water, and water freezing back into ice. Now think of a slice of bread turning into toast under the grill. One of these can be undone to get exactly what you started with, and one can't. Which is which — and, the important part, WHY can you undo one but not the other?
checkAnswer: Ice↔water is REVERSIBLE: melting and freezing just change the state; it's the same water, no new substance is made, so you can get the ice back by cooling. Bread→toast is IRREVERSIBLE: a new substance forms (you can't turn toast back into soft bread). The 'why' is the key: reversible changes make NO new material, so the change can run backwards.
